title: Generics
summary: A generic lets code keep track of a type chosen when the code is used.
introduction: A generic lets code keep track of a type chosen when the code is used. Think of a box that keeps the label of whatever you put inside. A helper can work with many kinds of values without forgetting their types.
learningObjectives: Write a generic function and explain how the compiler infers its type arguments
Constrain a type parameter with extends and relate two parameters with keyof
Declare generic interfaces and classes such as ApiResponse<T> and Stack<T>

blocks.text: `firstLoose` below accepts any array and returns `any`, so the caller gets no information back: `loose` can be used as a number, a string or a function without complaint. `first` declares a *type parameter* `T` in angle brackets, uses it for both the element type and the return type, and lets the compiler infer `T` from each call.

blocks.title: identity.ts
npx tsc identity.ts
blocks.content:
identity.ts:15:13 - error TS18048: 'num' is possibly 'undefined'.

15 console.log(num.toFixed(1));
               ~~~


Found 1 error in identity.ts:15

blocks.text: Hover over the variables: `loose` is `any`, `num` is `number | undefined`, `str` is `string | undefined`, and `explicit` is `boolean | undefined` because the type argument was written out for an empty array that offers nothing to infer from. The first `console.log` prints `1 1 a undefined`. The error on the last line is the generic version being *honest*: an empty array has no first element, and the return type says so, which `firstLoose` never could.

An unconstrained `T` could be anything, so inside the function you may not touch its properties. `extends` narrows what `T` can be. `T extends { length: number }` accepts strings, arrays and any object with a numeric `length`, and `a.length` becomes legal in the body while callers still get back exactly the type they passed in.

blocks.title: constraint.ts
npx tsc constraint.ts
blocks.content:
constraint.ts:8:9 - error TS2345: Argument of type 'number' is not assignable to parameter of type '{ length: number; }'.

8 longest(10, 20);
          ~~


Found 1 error in constraint.ts:8

blocks.text: The two valid calls print `apple` and `[ 1, 2 ]`, and their results are typed `string` and `number[]` rather than the constraint type. Numbers have no `length`, so the third call is rejected at the call site, before the body ever runs.

blocks.title: Common mistake: using T as if it had properties
blocks.text: `function describe<T>(value: T) { return value.length; }` fails with `TS2339: Property 'length' does not exist on type 'T'.` Beginners react by changing `T` to `any`, which throws away the type information generics exist to preserve. Add a constraint that names what you need (`T extends { length: number }`) or, if the function really does not care about the value, do not read its properties at all.

`keyof T` is the union of the property names of `T`. Constraining a second type parameter with `K extends keyof T` ties a key argument to the object argument, and the indexed access type `T[K]` is the type of that property. The result is a `pluck` function that knows that `pluck(user, "name")` returns a `string`.

blocks.title: keyof.ts
npx tsc keyof.ts
blocks.content:
keyof.ts:11:13 - error TS2345: Argument of type '"email"' is not assignable to parameter of type '"name" | "id" | "admin"'.

11 pluck(user, "email");
               ~~~~~~~


Found 1 error in keyof.ts:11

blocks.text: The valid lines print `ADA true`. Notice that `name.toUpperCase()` compiled: the compiler resolved `T[K]` to `string` for that call. Misspell a key and the error lists every real key, which is also what the editor's autocomplete offers as you type the quotes.

Type parameters work on interfaces and classes the same way. `ApiResponse<T>` describes an envelope whose `data` type varies per endpoint; `Stack<T>` is a container whose methods all share one `T`. You have been using generic types since the first lesson: `string[]` is `Array<string>`, and every `async` function returns a `Promise<T>`.

blocks.title: stack.ts
npx tsc stack.ts
blocks.content:
stack.ts:30:12 - error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.

30 stack.push("three");
              ~~~~~~~


Found 1 error in stack.ts:30

blocks.text: Without the last line the file prints `2 1` and then `2`. Because the class was instantiated as `Stack<number>`, every method is specialised: `push` accepts only numbers and `pop` returns `number | undefined`. Type parameters can also have defaults (`interface ApiResponse<T = unknown>`), and TypeScript 5.4 added `NoInfer<T>` for the rare case where one argument should not influence inference.

rows: Declare a type parameter and use it in the signature
Pass a type argument explicitly; usually inferred instead
`K` must be a property name of `T`
The type of property `K` in `T` (indexed access type)

blocks.title: Naming type parameters
blocks.text: `T` is conventional for a single parameter, `K` and `V` for keys and values, `E` for elements. In larger signatures prefer descriptive names such as `TItem` or `TResponse`; a generic with four single letters is hard to read six months later.

questions.question: What is the type of `result` in `const result = first(["x", "y"]);` given `function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined`?
questions.explanation: The compiler infers T as string from the array literal, so the return type T | undefined becomes string | undefined.

questions.question: In `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`, calling `get({ a: 1 }, "b")` is a compile error.
questions.explanation: keyof { a: number } is "a", so "b" does not satisfy the constraint on K and the compiler rejects the argument.
